sources.title: RIT CSCI-251 Concepts of Parallel and Distributed Systems catalog description
sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.content: This course is an introduction to the organization and programming of systems comprising multiple computers. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

sources.title: OpenMP API Specification
sources.author: OpenMP Architecture Review Board
sources.content: OpenMP defines a shared-memory parallel programming model based on directives, library routines, and environment variables. A parallel region creates a team of threads. Worksharing constructs divide loop iterations or sections among the team. Data-sharing attributes determine whether variables are shared, private, firstprivate, or reduced across threads. Barriers and other synchronization constructs establish ordering where independent execution is not sufficient. Incorrectly synchronized accesses can create data races. Scheduling choices influence load balance, locality, and overhead. Parallel analysis distinguishes available concurrency, task granularity, dependencies, synchronization cost, memory behavior, and measured scalability.

sources.title: MPI 4.1 Standard
sources.author: Message Passing Interface Forum
sources.content: MPI defines communication among processes identified by ranks in communicators. Point-to-point operations send and receive typed messages between selected ranks. Collective operations coordinate communication patterns such as broadcast, reduction, gather, scatter, and barrier across a group. Blocking and nonblocking operations expose different completion and overlap behavior. Message matching depends on communicator, source, and tag. Distributed-memory programs must partition data and work, communicate required dependencies, and avoid deadlock. Performance analysis considers communication volume, latency, load balance, synchronization, process placement, and the ratio of useful work to coordination overhead.
